title: Bathys: Advancing Deep Search Agents
abstract: Deep search is a critical capability for agents tackling complex, open-ended tasks, where solving a problem requires iterative information gathering, query reformulation, and evidence-based verification rather than a single retrieval step. To address these requirements, we present Bathys 9B and 27B deep search agents built around a training framework that spans verifiable question synthesis, post-training, and online reinforcement learning (RL) under context compression. Our high-quality data construction ensures both search depth and reliability: each clue is reformulated as an indirect reference requiring independent retrieval, and retained evidence chains enable verification that the clues jointly determine a unique answer. Curated trajectories underpin a pipeline of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO), and Compaction-Managed Group Sequence Policy Optimization (CM-GSPO): SFT provides a stable foundation for tool use over long horizons and query reformulation; KTO uses binary feedback on trajectories to improve the selection of answers grounded in evidence; CM-GSPO optimizes execution sub-trajectories with length-normalized likelihood ratios on the recorded rollout contexts and reweights sub-trajectory advantages to correct the extra weighting introduced by independently averaging sub-trajectory losses. Bathys 9B and 27B attain 66.51% and 80.49% on BrowseComp, respectively, under an evaluation protocol with trajectory self-verification and conditional retries.

title: How Classification Models Degrade as Data Diminish: A Multi-Criteria Analysis of Tabular Classifiers Under Controlled Data Scarcity
abstract: Machine learning research is frequently conducted under an implicit assumption of data abundance, yet applied software development often proceeds under severe data constraints. This study evaluated how five widely used classification algorithms—logistic regression, support vector machines, Gaussian naive Bayes, decision trees, and random forests—degrade when training data are systematically reduced. Eight tabular datasets drawn from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, spanning small, medium, and large volume tiers, were analysed within a quantitative comparative experimental design. Training folds were reduced to 100%, 75%, 50%, and 25% of their original size through stratified fractional sampling inside a stratified five-fold cross-validation loop, while validation folds were retained at full volume. Ten criteria were recorded: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, AUC-ROC, AUC-PR, mean absolute error and mean squared error of predicted probabilities, training time, and interpretability. One-way analyses of variance and Tukey honestly significant difference tests were applied at an alpha level of .05. Between-model differences were statistically significant in 31 of 32 dataset-by-volume configurations. Tree-based models exhibited the largest reductions in accuracy and the steepest increases in calibration error under scarcity, whereas logistic regression preserved threshold balance and probability calibration at negligible computational cost. Random forests attained the highest scores only when data were abundant. Pairwise comparisons aggregated across datasets were not significant, indicating that dataset context, rather than architectural complexity alone, governs absolute performance.

title: Read My Lips: Context-aware Lip Reading Using Language and Audio-Visual Models
abstract: Real-world speech is often partially observable: audio may be missing or corrupted by noise and competing speakers, while the speaker's lips remain visible. Recovering speech requires combining what can be heard, seen, and inferred from context. We introduce RML (Read My Lips), a collaborative method combining a lip reader, a language model, and an audio-visual generative model. The lip reader provides articulation hypotheses, the language model uses context to resolve ambiguous or missing words, and the audio-visual generator reconstructs synchronized speech while preserving speaker identity. Since source reliability varies, RML generates multiple reconstructions and uses the available evidence to favor the most reliable ones. This allows RML to handle missing audio, strong interference, and poor visual evidence without manually defined thresholds. Quantitative and qualitative experiments across these conditions show the benefit of combining visual, acoustic, and linguistic signals.

title: ICLWorld: Benchmarking In-Context Learning of Agents from Digital to Physical Worlds
abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets agents acquire new rules from context and adapt to user-specific requirements at inference time. The same frontier agents now operate both computers and robots, yet their ICL remains insufficiently assessed: existing benchmarks are largely offline, rely on text or static images, and risk training-data contamination, while robot evaluations are limited to method-level ablations. We present ICLWorld, an online benchmark that evaluates the ICL of agents from digital to physical worlds, covering computer use and robot use, together with UIverse, a unified harness that turns every environment into a user interface. We build 30 environments, record 630 demonstration videos (10+ hours), and design 160 tasks with customized, often counter-intuitive rules that cannot be satisfied without learning from the context. Each task comes with three rule versions, given as text or video, and we test generalization at three levels, from replaying the demonstration to new instances and unseen environments. Across six frontier models, the strongest agents, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, succeed on 82% and 76% of computer-use runs but only 27% and 26% of robot-use runs, and a no-rule control reduces success to at most 8%. GPT-6 Astra succeeds under all three rule versions on only 38% of computer-use tasks, half its rate under a single rule, and answers 98% of robot rule questions correctly yet completes only 20% of these tasks. Frontier agents learn rules comparably well from video and from text and transfer them across environments, whereas weaker agents rely on text and lose most of their video-based success once the demonstrated situation is resampled. These findings reveal substantial gaps between the digital and the physical world and between identifying a rule and acting on it.

title: Draft Calibration for Speculative Decoding: Accelerating LLM Serving by Matching Draft and Target Distributions
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by employing a lightweight draft model to propose draft tokens and allowing the target model to verify the new tokens in parallel to improve inference-time compute utilization. The speedup relies on the acceptance probability of draft tokens in target verification, which is directly related to the gap $\|p-q\|_1$ between the target distribution $p$ and the draft distribution $q$. In this paper, we study draft calibration of speculative decoding to improve the speedup of speculative decoding, where we employ post-hoc methods to calibrate the draft distribution to mitigate the distribution gap. We observe that though current community open-source draft models may learn the top candidate token correctly, they are generally underconfident compared to the target model, suggesting a consistent distribution mismatch. To mitigate the effect of this mismatch on the acceptance rate of the draft models, we try various post-hoc calibration methods, including standard temperature scaling and token-wise calibration. Our results suggest that a standard temperature scaling applied to the draft distribution improves the acceptance length by up to approximately 10\% with almost no additional cost across different tasks. Throughput analysis further verifies that this improvement in serving efficiency. Analysis of more general calibration methods reveals further potential room for improvement.

title: TeamFlowRL: Online Policy Optimization of Decentralized Flow Policies for Multi-Agent Coordination
abstract: Complex cooperative tasks require coordinated multi-agent behavior. Offline generative policies learn expressive cooperative behaviors from trajectories but remain limited by fixed datasets. Online reinforcement learning can improve them through environment interaction. However, fine-tuning flow policies is difficult because action likelihoods are hard to compute. We propose TeamFlowRL, a two-stage framework that pretrains multi-agent flow policies offline and fine-tunes them online. We formulate team policy optimization over the complete denoising trajectories of decentralized flow policies, avoiding intractable action likelihoods. The resulting objective weights each agent's trajectory ratio with a shared team advantage and clips each ratio separately, aligning local policy updates with the common team return. Across 51 paired configurations in seven simulation groups, TeamFlowRL improves every offline initialization, with a 47.3% average gain in normalized score. It also achieves 33.1% higher average success under exploration noise than Gaussian-policy fine-tuning across 6 bimanual tasks.

We propose TeamFlowRL, a two-stage framework that pretrains multi-agent flow policies offline and fine-tunes them online. We formulate team policy optimization over the complete denoising trajectories of decentralized flow policies, avoiding intractable action likelihoods. The resulting objective weights each agent's trajectory ratio with a shared team advantage and clips each ratio separately, aligning local policy updates with the common team return. Across 51 paired configurations in seven simulation groups, TeamFlowRL improves every offline initialization, with a 47.3% average gain in normalized score. It also achieves 33.1% higher average success under exploration noise than Gaussian-policy fine-tuning across 6 bimanual tasks.

title: S³: A Multicriteria Pre-Deployment Scoring Protocol for Enterprise Small Language Model Selection
abstract: Technology managers lack a systematic protocol for determining which enterprise workloads are safe for local small language model deployment. We introduce S³ (Suitability Score for SLM Selection), a multicriteria framework that scores workloads across six dimensions, Task Complexity, Output Structure, Stakeholder Risk, Data Sensitivity, Latency Tolerance, and Volume Load, and assigns them to Pure SLM, Hybrid, or LLM-Only tiers before inference. Non-compensatory gate rules enforce safety constraints for high-stakes scenarios, ensuring that life-critical or expert-level generative tasks are never assigned to a local model regardless of their aggregate score. Thresholds calibrated on an independent use-case set correctly predicted all eight held-out tier assignments across six industries, with Pure SLM tiers achieving at least 95% LLM parity.

title: Temporal Conditioning for Human Behavioral Cloning in Chess
abstract: Behavioral cloning models in chess typically predict human moves from board states while ignoring temporal inputs such as the remaining clock. However, time pressure is a major determinant of human decision-making quality, and temporal state is a missing dimension of human behavioral modeling. This paper introduces a time-aware transformer that extends a Chessformer-style architecture with learned temporal conditioning tokens encoding player clock state, time control, and recent tempo, together with behavioral heads for thinking time and resignation. The model is trained on large-scale online chess data and evaluated against time-agnostic baselines and the state of the art. Results show that temporal conditioning yields modest overall accuracy improvements but substantially stronger gains under time pressure. Beyond move choice, it also produces more accurate thinking-time and resignation predictions. More importantly, the model better matches human move-quality degradation in critical time regimes, reducing the systematic over-strength observed in time-agnostic behavioral cloning models. These results suggest that temporal state is a previously underutilized but important signal for human behavioral cloning in chess.

title: ReFocus: Progress-Guided Adaptive Practice for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables vision-language-action policies to improve through environmental interaction. However, in long-horizon manipulation, sparse success/failure feedback provides little information about where policies encounter bottlenecks. Moreover, repeated full-task rollouts also leave these bottlenecks weakly analyzed and insufficiently practiced. To this end, we introduce ReFocus, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates between Global and Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. Specifically, during Global RL, we decompose each task into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of subtasks. Then a DAG-based Progress Reward is leveraged for both policy training and bottleneck diagnosis. Based on the identified bottlenecks, ReFocus selects Adaptive Practice Windows, defining task segments from an entry stage to a target stage. It allocates additional interaction to these segments during Local RL while updating the entire policy. After that, it evaluates the policy to perform the full task for the next round of RL, forming an iteration between Global and Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus achieves success rates of 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively, compared with 90.6% and 39.3% for the π_{0.5} baseline. Furthermore, we evaluate a real-world adaptation on three long-horizon tasks. On BreadBaker, ReFocus achieves 95% success, compared with 30% for the π_{0.5}. Project page: https://refocus-robotics.github.io.

title: When AI grades higher: ethical concerns in algorithmic assessment
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the ethical implications of academic grading through the lens of epistemic justice. It investigates whether generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems introduce epistemic asymmetries that could challenge fairness, academic integrity and the governance of evaluative authority. Design/methodology/approach Eighty-seven undergraduate reports included in the study were evaluated by a faculty instructor and ChatGPT-4 using the same rubric. The analysis combined descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, Bland-Altman analysis and paired-samples t-tests. Divergence between instructor and AI scores may reflect differences in how the evaluation criteria are applied. Findings AI consistently assigned higher scores than the instructor and showed no meaningful correspondence in rankings. A systematic bias may suggest structural divergence in evaluative logic. Criterion-level correlations show that AI scoring follows more internally consistent patterns, whereas human judgements remain more differentiated, suggesting different grading standards. These results raise concerns about epistemic consistency in automated assessment. Practical implications The findings highlight the need for governance frameworks for AI grading. Institutions should define transparent policies, assign clear accountability and ensure structured human oversight to prevent algorithmic systems from controlling evaluative decisions. Originality/value This paper reconceptualises AI-mediated grading as an epistemic and governance issue rather than a technical procedure. It explores how automated systems may influence interpretations of academic merit. Empirical evidence of structural divergence between human and AI evaluative logics could support epistemic asymmetries. Integrating epistemic justice, the study provides a novel foundation for governing assessment systems.

title: Reinforcement Learning Can Be Recovered From Its Own Rollouts
abstract: Broadly speaking, reinforcement learning (RL) post-training converts compute into model capabilities by training on model-generated data. Typically, the rollouts are discarded after each update, and the knowledge acquired during RL resides in the model weights. In this work, we investigate how much of this knowledge is retained in the rollouts themselves. A natural first attempt is to replay the original RL algorithm on archived rather than freshly generated rollouts, but this leads to catastrophic collapse. We provide a simple explanation for this phenomenon, which in turn suggests a remedy: maximum likelihood on the archived rollouts. Surprisingly, starting from the same base model and replaying the rollouts in the order in which they were generated, without any distinction between correct and incorrect responses, is sufficient to recover the performance of online RL. In fact, a single maximum likelihood update per rollout batch closely tracks the entire learning curve of online RL. Furthermore, maximum likelihood on the rollouts of the last few RL steps often suffices to recover the final model's performance. This suggests that much of the compute invested in RL goes into discovering an improved sampling distribution rather than learning it from samples.

title: VenusOCR2.0: Towards Efficient and Effective Document Parsing
abstract: We present VenusOCR2.0, a compact 1B-parameter vision-language recognizer designed for both high-accuracy and high-throughput document parsing across text, tables, and formulas. To continuously improve recognition quality without self-training collapse, we build a bounded recursive self-improvement (RSI) data engine where the model acts strictly as a weakness probe, while external multi-expert medoid consensus, VLM visual verification, and factorized synthesis supply reliable supervision across pretraining, curated SFT, and RLVR. VenusOCR2.0 couples a dynamic-resolution SigLIP2 encoder and 2x2 spatial token merging with a Qwen3-0.6B decoder, adopting compact atomic OTSL tokens to shorten table sequences and reduce structural errors. To further eliminate the autoregressive decoding bottleneck, we introduce PTPv2, a lightweight (sim67M) decoupled parallel draft module that combines frozen multi-layer verifier conditioning, a standalone learned mask, and block-causal all-position next-token prediction. On OmniDocBenchv1.6, VenusOCR2.0 achieves an overall score of 96.45 and a state-of-the-art 98.57 formula CDM, substantially outperforming massive general-purpose VLMs such as Gemini-3-Pro (92.91) and Qwen3-VL-235B (89.78). Deployed in vLLM on a single H20 GPU, PTPv2 delivers a 2.96x single-request speedup and up to 2.36x higher batched throughput while guaranteeing lossless, token-for-token equivalence with standard autoregressive decoding.

title: Commentary: a practical response to the challenge of GenAI-Implementation for small business
abstract: Purpose This study aims to provide a response from a practitioner perspective on the articles in the special issue and provide insights and recommendations for small businesses to translate research into practice. Design/methodology/approach A conceptual approach is used, drawing on practice-informed insights. Findings This commentary identifies three key insights based on the articles in this special issue: (1) treat Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) like a new team member, (2) start with the customer, not the tool and (3) build capability through small-scale trials. Practical implications This commentary assists business chambers and small business by synthesising the key practical insights from articles in this special issue for use by small business. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this commentary is one of the first in an academic business journal to be the voice of small business on the topic of GenAI and small business.

title: GREMLIN: Generating Random Environments for Meta-Learning with Interacting Networks
abstract: Can randomly parameterized neural environments supply useful experience for learning a reinforcement learning algorithm? We investigate this question using DiscoRL's rule-discovery framework, replacing human-designed training games with sixteen selected neural environments. Each game combines bounded vector dynamics with a random strategy-based reward and an independent outcome reward. After 224.8 million agent-environment steps, we froze the teacher and trained fresh agents. DQN outscored GREMLIN on most games, both generated and human-designed. GREMLIN nevertheless outperformed the untrained teacher on all 26 games, showing that generated experience can improve a learning rule. It remains unclear whether this approach can yield a competitive rule with longer meta-training.

title: PartAgent: Agentic 3D Part Segmentation via Expert Integration and Closed-Loop Refinement
abstract: Segmenting a 3D object into semantically meaningful parts requires joint reasoning about geometric structure and semantic context. Pretrained 3D experts provide spatially grounded region proposals, while 2D experts provide semantic cues for identifying object parts. The challenge is to integrate these complementary capabilities into a framework that can both produce meaningful part segmentations and progressively refine them. We present PartAgent, a training-free agentic framework for 3D part segmentation built upon two complementary modules: (i) Structural-Semantic Expert Integration combines regions predicted by the 3D expert with multiview semantic evidence from the 2D expert through image-to-surface correspondences, constructing compositional part partitions at multiple granularities. (ii) Observation-Driven Closed-Loop Partition Refinement observes the current partition and its supporting evidence to select targeted inspection, evidence repair, composition, or reselection actions. It verifies proposed changes and uses the updated state and action outcomes to guide subsequent decisions. On PartObjaverse-Tiny-WT, PartAgent achieves 68.41 mIoU, outperforming the strongest competing method by 8.53 points. Across 3DCoMPaT200, PartNeXt, PartNetE, and PartObjaverse-Tiny, PartAgent achieves the highest mIoU on each dataset, averaging 69.36 across the four datasets, 7.28 points above the highest mean among competing methods.

title: Delegent: A Multi-Agent Harness That Reduces Cost without Sacrificing Performance
abstract: Agents built on frontier language models are expensive. At every step, the frontier model re-reads its entire context and executes every subtask regardless of its difficulty. This paper explores the simple thesis that much of this cost can be removed by delegating easy subtasks to a small language model, or SLM, that runs on hardware one already owns. To test it, we build Delegent, a simple and effective agent harness built on Claude Code, in which the frontier model stays in charge of every task but hands focused subtasks, such as investigating code, running tests, and searching a corpus, to SLM subagents. Existing approaches such as cascades and model routers usually choose which model executes the entire task, whereas in Delegent, the frontier model always leads the execution and delegates easy subtasks to the SLM. No router or model is trained, so either model can be swapped freely. With the help of a 27B FP8 SLM, Delegent reduces the frontier cost of long-horizon coding by 67% and of agentic search by 59%, with no loss in task performance, and even a 2B SLM that fits on a laptop reduces the coding cost by 66%. The savings grow with the legwork that the frontier model would otherwise do itself, and a short instruction, which leaves the main coding tasks to the frontier model, accounts for most of the saving and keeps the 2B SLM from losing tasks. Code: https://github.com/castorini/delegent

title: Reliability-aware AI Agent Execution in Collaborative Edge Computing: A World Model Approach
abstract: Collaborative edge computing supports AI agent applications by distributing execution across heterogeneous user-controlled devices with limited resources. This paper studies reliability-aware AI agent execution under node failures and wireless disruptions. These disruptions can make agent execution state unavailable or inconsistent, forcing recovery or recomputation that consumes the remaining deadline budget. Maintaining recoverable execution states can therefore improve request completion before deadlines. We formulate an online AI agent execution management problem that jointly selects resource allocations, state protection actions, and recovery targets to maximize the expected task success rate subject to resource, compatibility, and deadline constraints. We develop a world model that jointly captures evolving agent workflows and recoverable execution state under candidate management actions, accounting for node reliability, network conditions, and resource availability. The model enables the controller to simulate future execution and recovery trajectories under candidate actions and estimate their effects on execution progress and task completion before deadlines. We then employ world model-based model predictive control (WorldMPC) with Monte Carlo rollouts to jointly optimize resource allocation, state protection, and recovery decisions for long-term reliable agent execution under the dynamic environment. We evaluate the proposed approach on the simulation and real-world testbed using real-world and synthetic datasets. Experimental results show that WorldMPC improves task success rate over baselines in both simulation and real-world testbed.

title: EventDiffusion: Learning Native Event Stream Distribution from Videos
abstract: Event cameras capture asynchronous brightness changes at high temporal resolution, but scarce recordings constrain data-driven research. Sparse RGB observations cannot uniquely determine intervening events since identical frames may correspond to streams with different activity, polarities, and timing. Existing simulators largely rely on prescribed sensor dynamics and estimated brightness trajectories, whose assumptions limit the diversity and fidelity of plausible event streams. We introduce EventDiffusion, a hierarchical generative framework that directly learns the conditional distribution of native asynchronous event streams from real recordings. EventDiffusion decomposes generation into three probabilistic processes: Event Activity Diffusion (EAD) learns stochastic discrete event counts; Event Spatial Allocation (ESA) distributes these counts to individual pixels while preserving cardinality; and Event Timing Diffusion (ETD) learns continuous asynchronous timestamp distributions. We also introduce CEFS, an event-stream realism metric combining event activity and polarity with multiscale space-time structure and temporal fidelity. Across all datasets, EventDiffusion achieves double the accuracy of SOTA methods and demonstrates robustness across different cameras at any resolution.

title: HS-OVSeg: Multi-Granularity Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation in Remote Sensing via Heterogeneous Supervision
abstract: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) enables flexible, text-driven mapping of remote sensing (RS) imagery beyond predefined categories. Despite advances in segmentation foundation models, RS-OVSS remains constrained by the scarcity of large-scale, semantically diverse datasets with accurate pixel-level annotations. Meanwhile, existing RS datasets contain abundant scene- and object-level annotations that offer valuable semantic information but lack precise pixel-wise supervision. To exploit these complementary sources, we propose HS-OVSeg, a unified training framework that integrates heterogeneous scene-, object-, and pixel-level supervision for RS-OVSS. Specifically, we generate pixel-wise pseudo-labels using SAM3, conditioned on scene-level class names and object-level class names with bounding boxes. Combined with ground-truth semantic masks, these pseudo-labels enable joint training across all three annotation granularities through LoRA-based fine-tuning of SAM3. Our unified training spans 20 RS datasets, including 3 scene classification, 4 object detection, and 13 semantic segmentation datasets, with 1,000 images from the 7 classification and detection datasets manually annotated for pixel-level evaluation. HS-OVSeg substantially outperforms existing RS-OVSS models across both the 20 training-source and 5 held-out datasets, demonstrating strong multi-granularity segmentation capabilities under heterogeneous supervision. The code will be publicly available upon publication.

title: AIChipBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Automated AI Accelerator Design
abstract: A language-model decoder carries state between decoding steps, and in hardware a wrong state update can leave the current token correct and corrupt the output several tokens later, so a design can pass output tests and still be wrong. AIChipBench asks what LLM coding agents need to build such hardware correctly. Agents implement quantized Qwen3.5, Gemma 3, Gemma 4, and Llama 3.2 decoders in synthesizable register-transfer-level (RTL) code against an executable integer reference that specifies the outputs and the stored state at every decoding step. They debug against public tests under fixed budgets; their frozen designs are graded on held-out token sequences, resets, memory stalls, and synthesis, and a second track asks them to speed up a correct design at nearly fixed area. Across 9,136 attempts by four coding agents, the difficulty lies in stored state. Feedback that points to the first state mismatch raises acceptance over output-only feedback in all 12 agent--task cells of a matched study, by 25.0 to 46.9 percentage points, and halves the agent-hours per accepted design. Regraded on new sequences and conditions, 45 of 69 accepted designs fail within the 32 steps their tests required. More than a third of attempts to speed up a correct design end without one. An overall score ranks Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5, and both halves of the instances give this order in all 200 random splits. Hardware agents therefore need debugging feedback that exposes stored state, and their benchmarks need final tests well beyond the development cases.

title: X-3DComposer: Feed-Forward 3D Scene Composition with Any Assets from Any Views
abstract: Composing an editable 3D scene from images requires an asset for each object and a layout that places the assets. 3D generation and CAD retrieval now supply the assets, but layout still lacks a general solution: scene generation methods couple it with generation, and pose estimators handle one object at a time and need true-size CAD models, depth, or iterative refinement. We present X-3DComposer, a feed-forward model that predicts the layout separately from asset generation. Given one or more images of a scene, the object masks, and an asset for each object from any source, it jointly predicts the rotation, translation, and per-axis scale of all objects in a single forward pass of about one second. The key idea is to treat objects as views: renders of the assets are processed together with the scene images by a multi-view geometry model adapted from VGGT-Ω, and each object pose follows in closed form from the cameras predicted for its renders. Camera intrinsics, camera poses, and depth are optional inputs. When the meshes produced by five scene generation methods are kept fixed and only their layout is replaced, the layouts of X-3DComposer are more accurate than the native layouts of these methods. Compared with the stand-alone layout model SceneMaker, it reduces the scene-level Chamfer distance by 52% on IndoorMix, our test set from six indoor datasets, and by 28% on 3D-FUTURE.

title: The Radar-based Activities of Daily Living (R-ADL) Dataset
abstract: Monitoring Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) supports safety and well-being for people living at home, especially older adults, and radar sensing is gaining increasing attention in the field of activity recognition for its ability to ensure privacy in the home while also surpassing technical limitations of other sensing modalities. However, radar-based activity recognition remains constrained by the limited availability of large-scale datasets. We introduce the Radar-based Activities of Daily Living (R-ADL) dataset to addresses the gaps identified in existing work: 1) it expands the scale of available data by providing over eight hours of annotated recordings in which a person performs eight distinct activities; 2) it overcomes room configuration limitations by recording from five different locations in a two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment; and 3) it extends beyond primitive actions to focus on high-level ADLs. In addition to the dataset, this paper introduces practical guidance for future ADL dataset construction. We conducted a detailed analysis of how ADLs are prioritized across academic research, health survey tools, and clinical trials to identify clinically significant ADLs. Furthermore, we provide our experimental design, data collection and annotation strategies, post-processing pipeline for forming the R-ADL dataset from raw data, and baseline results on standard machine learning architectures. The R-ADL dataset serves as a valuable resource for advancing ADL recognition systems as we continue building larger and more diverse datasets.

title: MAGPIE: Agentic Multi-Reference Image Generation via Executable Scene Construction
abstract: Multi-reference image generation requires a model to preserve the appearance of selected subjects while arranging them according to an instruction. Despite recent progress in reference-based generation and compositional control, reliably organizing selected subjects into the intended scene remains challenging. Although existing methods provide various forms of compositional guidance, the planned relationships are not always explicitly instantiated for inspection and refinement before image synthesis. To address this limitation, we introduce MAGPIE, which represents the intended composition as a simplified 3D scene defined by an executable Blender program. A coding agent links each scene instance to its reference, checks the geometry and rendered view against the instruction, and revises the program to correct discrepancies. The final proxy rendering serves as a visual plan for the image generator. Using MAGPIE-Instruct-3K, we train the generator to follow this plan while drawing each subject's appearance from its reference. MAGPIE improves both Qwen and FLUX on DreamOmni2 and SconeEval. With FLUX, it improves overall success on DreamOmni2 by 28.21 percentage points over the original backbone and achieves the highest overall score among the models evaluated on SconeEval.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Candidate Generation for Entity Linking in Cyber Threat Intelligence
abstract: Entity Resolution (ER) pipelines often collapse ambiguity into early hard decisions: upstream Named Entity Recognition (NER) selects a single span and type, and downstream Entity Linking (EL) treats that choice as ground truth. This discards valuable information about the ambiguity of the underlying data (e.g., span boundary disagreement and type confusion), leading to brittle systems that fail unpredictably when faced with uncertainty in inputs. Therefore, this work presents a proof-of-concept for uncertainty-aware ER that treats uncertainty as native data that should be preserved and exploited throughout ER pipelines. We (i) capture uncertainty signals in the NER stage and (ii) leverage these signals into the EL stage to improve candidate retrieval under ambiguity. Using a BERT-based NER model augmented with two auxiliary span-boundary prediction heads, we apply Monte Carlo (MC) dropout at inference time to derive three mention-level proxy signals: the MC-averaged start-boundary probability, the MC-averaged end-boundary probability, and De Luca-Termini fuzzy entropy computed over the Begin-Inside-Outside (BIO) predictive distribution. These signals are used to adapt the fuzzy cutoff in candidate generation (CG) for EL. Because CG is treated as a blocking step, we evaluate retrieval recall. On the AnnoCTR dataset linked to the MITRE ATTCK knowledge base, the boundary-aware and dual-signal fuzzy linking approaches improve Recall@10 from 0.6186 to 0.7966. The contribution lies not in an end-to-end optimised ER pipeline but in establishing uncertainty preservation as a viable and beneficial component of ER pipelines, enabling downstream EL to make better-informed decisions under uncertainty.

title: Factorized Context Attention: From Emulated to Native Grid Probing
abstract: Models read a book, an hour of video, or an image in one forward pass. As the context grows, this pass slows down, loses accuracy, and stops at the context window. Sparse attention is efficient, but keeps the other two limitations. Grid probing, a recent training-free method, recovers the accuracy and extends the reach by asking a frozen model the same question about short local and strided spans of the input, but every question repeats the whole computation, since each span is encoded again. Our insight is that grid probing is emulated attention, an attention pattern reproduced from outside the model through prompts, since each probe only restricts which part of the input the question can see. We introduce Factorized Context Attention (FCA), a training-free block-sparse attention that runs the same pattern natively, as the attention of the model itself. FCA encodes the input once into a KV cache, reads all spans as masked sequences in one batched forward, and uses a stair position schedule to keep every span inside the trained position range. Across long video understanding, long-context text inference and image grounding, FCA matches the accuracy and the reach of grid probing at a fraction of its cost. It gains about 10 points over the single pass on long video and 9 to 14 points on long novels, finds needles in videos of over a thousand frames and in texts four times the length of the window, and answers a later question about the same input in as little as a tenth of the time of grid probing. Native attention thus keeps what emulated attention gains without its cost, all with existing frozen language and vision-language models.

title: Shifter Quantization: Compact Representations for Native Integer Computation
abstract: Groupwise quantization is used in LLM quantization to improve accuracy at low bit widths, but grouping weights keeps standard integer MMA from spanning the full dot product for efficient GPU inference. We develop a new quantization method, Shifter Quantization (SQ), that reconstructs native-width integer operands by appending and shifting shared bits. To further extend the efficiency, we develop a special variant of SQ, Shifter Integer (SHI), to use INT4 kernels. We show that SQ and SHI formats perform better than standard groupwise quantization in quality, as measured by projection error and KL divergence, and in inference speed, as measured during decoding and prefill. For low precision like 2-bit quantization, SQ2 and SHI2 achieve 2.71-3.77x the 4,096-token prefill throughput of llama.cpp on a Q2_K checkpoint and reduce WikiText-2 KL by 6.6-7.8%. For mid precision like 4-bit quantization, SQ4 achieves 1.43-2.47x the prefill throughput of NInfer's groupwise-integer baselines across the tested models and prompt lengths, with 24-40% lower KL than the NInfer baselines. For high precision like 8-bit quantization, SQ8 achieves 27.4% higher batch-one prefill throughput and 72.7% lower KL than vLLM's online FP8.

title: Fractal Neural Synthesis: Constant-Storage Procedural Weight Derivation via Complex Quadratic Boundary Dynamics
abstract: Conventional neural networks store synaptic parameters as explicit tensors whose persistent Flash footprint scales linearly (O(W)) with parameter count, constraining resource-limited edge microcontrollers. We formulate and systematically evaluate Fractal Neural Synthesis (FNS), a procedural weight derivation architecture that replaces hidden-layer matrices with a constant 24-byte coordinate seed Theta = (c_x, c_y, ell) in F_64^3 anchored near the complex quadratic bifurcation boundary dM of f_c(z) = z^2 + c. We introduce a large-bailout (R = 256) smooth escape kernel, four zero-overhead geometric sampling apertures--Cartesian Grid, coprime 3x3 Rule-of-Thirds (Z/9Z), phi-Vogel spiral, and multi-scale Harmonic Tripod--and prove conditional Kolmogorov (K_Kolm <= 192 + c_0 bits) and Shannon entropy bounds. Across magnifications zeta in [10^0, 10^8], C^1 Fourier and lattice-noise bases collapse to post-standardization rank ~2.25 and SHA-256 PRNG exhibits avalanche discontinuity (rho ~ 0.019, 50.6% micro-step retention), whereas dM uniquely sustains both rank (~10.0) and local continuity (rho in [0.81, 0.97], 89.2% retention). Under leak-free 10-fold CV across four zero-scaler-byte non-linear benchmarks, FNS with an INT8 readout surpasses 0-hidden Linear-INT8 by +3.6 to +10.8 pp while delivering 10.7x-129x total Flash reduction (725x-2,773x hidden reduction) relative to converged Float32 MLPs (90.30% Ionosphere in 285 B; 97.22% Optical Digits in 2,598 B; 97.90% PenDigits in 2,598 B; 87.00% Satimage in 1,570 B).

title: FOL-Proof: Verifying LLM Text-to-Logic Translations via Deterministic Semantics
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate natural-language statements into first-order logic (FOL) to improve reasoning. However, LLMs are prone to errors, and so a semantically unfaithful FOL formula could corrupt downstream reasoning. We present FOL-Proof, a semantic firewall pipeline that validates LLM-generated FOL translations against independently derived linguistic interpretations. FOL-Proof operates by deterministically obtaining a pool of candidate translations via semantic analysis tools, such as the English Resource Grammar and Minimal Recursion Semantics; then applying an SMT solver to check each derived reading for logical equivalence to the LLM-generated formula. If the translation is faithful it is accepted; otherwise, it is rejected, or optionally repaired via repeated invocations to the LLM. The procedure is conservative: incomplete search, unsupported constructions, or inconclusive checks yield abstention rather than false rejection. We evaluated FOL-Proof on established benchmarks (ProofWriter, RuleTaker and PrOntoQA), and also on a new adversarial benchmark (LongFaithCheck). Our experiments show that FOL-Proof attains near perfect selective accuracy, while direct LLM judges and round-trip baselines show substantially worse performance.

title: LookAnything: A Foundation Model for Holistic Gaze Following
abstract: Human gaze provides a rich window into attention and intent, making its understanding essential for applications ranging from social signal analysis to human-robot interaction. Existing methods typically employ highly customized architectures relying on auxiliary inputs like head crops or depth maps, causing cascading errors and inference overhead. Trained on single domains and confined to isolated gaze following with heatmap outputs, they lack flexibility and generalization for diverse interactive scenarios. To bridge this gap, we present LookAnything, a foundation model that unifies diverse gaze-centric tasks for holistic gaze following. Benefiting from large-scale multi-task and cross-domain training, LookAnything flexibly adapts to various settings, generating diverse outputs (points, boxes, heatmaps, and language) and supporting broad gaze-centric localization, description, and reasoning. At its core, we introduce learnable gaze-prior queries to promote gaze-aware representation learning, eliminating the need for auxiliary external inputs. To facilitate this paradigm, we construct HoliGaze, a comprehensive corpus and benchmark comprising 311K question-answer pairs across 5 capability dimensions and 9 distinct tasks. Experiments demonstrate that LookAnything consistently outperforms 33 leading vision-language models on holistic gaze following, while remaining highly competitive with dedicated specialists across 5 conventional target detection benchmarks. Evaluation on unseen datasets and deployment on a real robot further validate its strong out-of-domain generalization and flexible adaptation in real-world scenarios.

title: On the Creation of Object-Centric Event Logs from Patient Journeys
abstract: Interactions between patients and health systems as well as conditions that individuals experience during a disease are represented in patient journeys. Therefore, patient journeys are important assets to investigate how care is being provided, and how health systems can be designed to better suit the needs of patients. While there is initial work on patient journeys from a process mining perspective with traditional case notions, object-centric process mining techniques have yet to be covered. This is unfortunate, since due to the rich structure of objects and their relationships, object-centric process mining approaches are particularly promising in this context. This paper addresses this gap by investigating object-centric event log (OCEL) generation from patient journeys. Based on a list of challenges and requirements, the paper presents an approach for the creation of OCELs from patient journey data. The approach is evaluated on a synthetic patient cohort provided by our industry partner.

title: GOLD-SLAM: Gaussian-splatting Omnidirectional LiDAR-Depth SLAM
abstract: Panoramic cameras capture nearly the entire spherical field of view in a single frame. However, the mismatch between this panoramic coverage and the field of view of LiDAR poses a substantial challenge for panoramic Gaussian splatting SLAM that relies on LiDAR depth priors. We introduce GOLD-SLAM, a Gaussian-splatting Omnidirectional LiDAR-Depth SLAM system that combines high-quality rendering with accurate geometric reconstruction. It performs tracking and mapping in the spherical domain and uses tracked visual features in regions without LiDAR coverage to improve pose estimation. To address insufficient coverage of newly observed surfaces and floating artifacts during incremental mapping, we introduce Depth-Aware Map Extension and Pruning (DAEP). To enable broader evaluation, we collect a new dataset, WHOLE, using a UAV platform across Weak-geometry, High-dynamic, Omnidirectional, Low-light, and Easy scenarios. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks and WHOLE demonstrate competitive rendering quality and improved geometric accuracy relative to perspective systems. title: The Reliability Function of Error-Correcting Output Codes with Noisy Binary Classifiers
abstract: Error-correcting output coding (ECOC) builds a multi-class classifier from binary classifiers. We study the excess error rate of ECOC over the Bayes (MAP) classifier when each binary classifier outputs a posterior estimate whose log-odds is corrupted by Gaussian noise. Recasting decoding as a test over a Gaussian channel, we derive an upper bound from the union and Chernoff bounds and a lower bound from the nearest competing category and the Mills ratio. The bounds show that a large Hamming distance is both necessary and sufficient for reducing the excess error rate. The excess error rate stays bounded away from zero, by a constant that depends on the two largest posteriors and the noise level but not on the number of categories $M$, whenever the distance between the code words of the two most probable categories is bounded; for equidistant codes this distance is $d_{\min}$. Conversely, it is at most $M-1$ times a factor that is exponentially small in the minimum distance $d_{\min}$, and it vanishes whenever $κ\,d_{\min}-\ln(M-1)\to\infty$ for an explicit $κ$ (for general codes, under a posterior condition). For $n$-vs-rest codes with $n\geq2$, the upper and lower exponents coincide asymptotically, which determines the reliability function of ECOC in closed form. The results extend to correlated Gaussian noise with the Hamming distance replaced by an effective distance; when noise is shared at the level of categories, the effective distance stays bounded and the excess error rate does not vanish for any code. All theorems are machine-checked in Lean 4. In a semi-synthetic setting, the measured decay agrees with the predicted exponent. On ResNet-50 features of CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet-1k, the excess error over a log-likelihood decoding reference decreases with $d_{\min}$ and, for larger $M$, levels off at a moderate distance, while codes with $d_{\min}=1$ degrade as $M$ grows.

title: ASTERISM: Do Multimodal LLMs Actually Look at All the Images?
abstract: Multi-image benchmarks aim to test whether a multimodal large language model (MLLM) combines evidence across images, but many of their items can be answered from a single image. Across about 33k items from 19 public benchmarks, our audit and a two-stage single-image filter find that one image or the question alone settles 24.2% of them. On these items, MLLMs recover from one image a median 78% of the accuracy that all images add over the text alone, so these items reward answering from one image, which we call the single-image shortcut. MLLMs take this shortcut even on items where one image is not enough. On such items, most of their wrong answers repeat an answer they give from one image, at a rate well above chance. We build ASTERISM, to our knowledge the largest audited multi-image benchmark, from these 19 benchmarks by keeping their items that need more than one image. Its 18.7k items, 2.0k of them corrected or rewritten, share one format, one scorer and seven task categories. We also release ASTERISM-Train with 49k training items and ASTERISM-Lite, a hard subset whose items we manually verify one by one. On ASTERISM-Lite, the strongest proprietary MLLM scores 68%. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), now common in MLLM post-training, rewards the shortcut as well, because a correct answer read off one image earns as much reward as one that combines images. In line with this, existing RLVR objectives add little to the ASTERISM score. To stop rewarding the shortcut in training as ASTERISM does in evaluation, we propose cross-image credit assignment (CICA), an extension of RLVR that moves the credit toward the tokens that need more than one image. On three open-source MLLMs, CICA raises the ASTERISM score by 2.6 to 6.0 points, more than twice the gain of each general and vision-specific RL objective trained on the same data.

title: Auditing the Judge: Human-Derived Bias Discovery, Quantification, and Mitigation in LLM Judges
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as automated evaluators in evaluation and training pipelines, their judgements are often affected by systematic biases that conflict with human preferences. Although prior work has identified various biases and proposed methods for detecting and mitigating them, less attention has been paid to using human preferences to inform bias identification and mitigation. Moreover, these approaches rely heavily on pre-discovered bias lists, overlook bias strength, and depend on costly interventions. In this work, we propose HUB-J, an integrated framework based on human-derived bias factors that detects, quantifies, and mitigates biases in LLM-as-a-Judge systems. Our approach leverages human-LLM judgement disagreement cases to automatically discover interpretable bias factors, and utilizes agreement cases to quantify bias strength through controlled input modifications and resulting shifts in model decisions. Finally, building on these quantified biases, we introduce a lightweight, training-free regression-based mitigation strategy that estimates the influence of each bias factor on model judgments and corrects bias-influenced decisions by removing its estimated effect. Empirical results show that HUB-J uncovers both known and novel bias factors, reveals meaningful differences in model susceptibility, and consistently reduces bias-driven decision flips while generalizing across models.

title: Reproducing the Speech Labels of Qwen3-Omni's Talker: Mimi in bf16, and a Last-Frame Pitfall
abstract: Qwen3-Omni speaks through a Talker predicting 16 codebooks of a 12.5 Hz audio codec, but the encoder that made its training labels was not released, so new voices cannot be trained on matching labels. We identify this encoder from the released model's behavior. White-box regression shows that the codebook embeddings of the Talker, its multi-token predictor and the Code2Wav decoder match the first 16 codebooks of kyutai's Mimi layer by layer. A decoder-based test looks convincing but fails calibration: decoders trained on known labels cannot tell them apart. Teacher-forced Talker likelihoods, calibrated with 13 code language models trained on known labels, do tell implementations apart: the Talker prefers labels from kyutai's moshi package with bf16 weights over every other variant we tried. Loudness normalization and band-limiting of 20% or more of the data are ruled out. Separately, transformers' MimiModel encodes the last frame differently from kyutai's encoder unless the input length is a multiple of 1920 samples. After LoRA fine-tuning on its labels, 44--55% of generated sentences end in a noise burst, and the same frame costs the Mimi-based CSM-1B 119 nats; padding the input removes both. We release the encoding recipe, a label checker and a Talker fine-tuning toolkit.

title: U-Statistics-Powered LLM Reasoning
abstract: Since its introduction by DeepSeek, group relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been widely adopted for training large reasoning models and agents, spurring a proliferation of its variants. Yet the group size, a crucial hyperparameter in these GRPO-type algorithms, remains largely chosen by trial and error. Exploiting the U-statistic structure of GRPO's policy gradient, we recast the selection of the group size as a classical statistical problem of variance ratio estimation. This problem is particularly challenging when the denominator of the ratio is small, rendering naive plug-in estimators unstable. To address this challenge, we propose a pessimistic ratio estimator that accounts for the denominator's estimation uncertainty. We characterise the statistical properties of this estimator across three sample-size regimes. Empirically, using %a jackknife-based pessimistic rule on synthetic tasks from Reasoning Gym and real-world benchmarks covering both mathematical reasoning and code generation, we show that our adaptive group size selection reduces the mean squared error of the resulting policy gradient and improves policy optimisation over fixed-group-size baselines, with modest additional computational cost.

title: RoboDemo: Reconciling Demonstration Intent and Execution Progress for Long-Horizon Manipulation
abstract: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires more than predicting the next action from the current observation. The policy must maintain a global procedural prior that specifies the expected progress of each subtask stage, while also tracking the realized progress produced by its interactions. To this end, we propose RoboDemo, a demonstration-augmented manipulation framework built on Dual-Cascaded Test-Time-Training. RoboDemo accepts either a task-relevant human demonstration video or a semantically compatible robot video retrieved from simulation corpus as reference, allowing us to evaluate its applicability with and without paired human demonstrations. Task semantics and physical motion information from the reference video are then transferred into persistent demonstration-intent memory. During deployment, we causally compress online observations, robot states, and executed actions into interaction-progress memory. To keep reference intent stable while interaction progress continually evolves, reference and execution video tokens independently update their respective fast-weight states. The action expert performs cascaded memory reads, first obtaining reference guidance and then refining it using realized progress, allowing the policy to adapt to execution deviations without overwriting the stored intent. RoboDemo achieves 90.7% success on Imitator Game and 73.3% success across three real-world household tasks. Real-world videos, code and hf-weights are available in our project website.

title: cxr-selective-trust: reproducibility audit tooling and frozen-prediction artifacts for medical vision-language model evaluation
abstract: Audit tooling and frozen-prediction artifacts for measuring medical vision-language models (VLMs). The repository contains two manuscripts, the protocols and configs that produced them, and cxr-audit, a CPU-only command-line tool that recomputes the denominator of a prediction file (rows, unique keys, duplicate rows/groups, parse rate), measures response collapse and P1 change on shifted inputs, and compares selective-prediction signals (status-aware confidence, Bernoulli entropy, probability margin) by AUROC and coverage at fixed risk budgets. No model weights, medical images or patient data are redistributed. Code, manifests and derived tables are MIT-licensed; the original dataset and model licences continue to apply. The manuscripts are "Responsiveness Before Reliance: Four Reversals in Measuring Medical Vision-Language Models" and "Auditing the Denominator: Coverage Census and Fault-Tested Durability for Medical VLM Benchmarks". License boundary: the MIT license covers the code, manifests and derived tables only. The two manuscript PDFs in this archive are preprints, remain copyright (C) 2026 Koshun Huang, and are not covered by the MIT license. Model weights and medical images are not included.

title: Understanding Clipping In Zeroth-Order Optimization
abstract: Zeroth-order optimization has emerged as a resource-efficient alternative to Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) when fine-tuning LLMs, thanks to the inherent low dimensionality of the loss landscape. It relies on a two-point estimate of the gradient that only accesses the function value and not the gradient, bypassing the resource-heavy backpropagation. Recently, it was accidentally discovered that per-sample clipping can improve the performance of the trained model, while running a differentially private version of zeroth-order optimization \cite{zhang2024dpzero} with a very large privacy parameter $ε$ (corresponding to very little privacy). In this paper, we systematically investigate this phenomenon and demonstrate that ($i$) the optimal choice of learning rate $η$ is inversely proportional to the clipping threshold $c$, satisfying $ηc =$ constant; ($ii$) clipping drives the zeroth-order optimization to a different solution with higher test accuracy; and ($iii$) this phenomenon is only observed with per-sample clipped zeroth-order optimization and not other zeroth-order alternatives that also provide robust estimates of the gradient. Further analyses with artificially injected label noise reveals that clipping leads to more robust predictions, which stems from the implicit down weighting of hard-to-fit training examples. Our code is available at https://github.com/SewoongLab/ClipZero

title: CaveBench: Benchmarking Abductive Physical Reasoning from Internal Observations
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are advancing in physical reasoning, but whether they can understand external physical drivers from internal observations remains an open question. Existing benchmarks have not specifically targeted this setting. To this end, we introduce CaveBench, a benchmark for abductive physical reasoning from internal observations. Models receive apparatus descriptions and internal images while the external controls remain hidden, and must infer the operations responsible for the observed responses. CaveBench spans 20 apparatus scenes in five physical domains and contains 10,200 simulated episodes, split into 9,000 training, 1,000 validation, and 200 test episodes. Questions span one to six events and require the complete control set at every event, testing whether an explanation accounts for the entire process. Synchronized observations and control records provide the inputs and reference answers. Evaluating 27 VLM configurations yields six-event exact-match accuracies of 68.0% for the strongest closed-source model and 12.5% for the strongest open-weight model. Seven adaptation baselines show that single-event gains need not improve complete sequences. Error analysis identifies failures in visual identification, physical inference, evidence integration, and action composition, specifying where current models struggle to connect internal phenomena with their external causes.

title: PREreview of "EmergentTTS-Eval: Evaluating TTS Models on Complex Prosodic, Expressiveness, and Linguistic Challenges Using Model-as-a-Judge"
abstract: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/24485595. ## Summary This paper introduces EmergentTTS-Eval, a benchmark of 1,645 test items across six categories of difficult speech synthesis (emotions, paralinguistics, foreign words, questions, syntactic complexity, and complex pronunciation). Only 100 items are human-written seeds, taken from five categories of the previously published BASE-TTS sample set; the remaining 91.5% were generated or rewritten by large language models, including three rounds of "depth" rewrites applied to every base item. Each TTS system is scored by pairwise comparison against a single fixed baseline voice, with Gemini 2.5 Pro acting as an audio judge; the headline metric is a win rate against that baseline. The authors report that judge rankings correlate with human preference at Spearman ρ = 90.5%, and the benchmark has been accepted to the NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks track and is positioned for adoption as a community standard. My concerns are not with the topic, which is important, nor with the engineering effort, which is substantial. They are with the validation chain: at almost every step where the benchmark asks to be trusted — item generation, judging, human alignment, and score stability — the verifying party is either the same model, a very small sample, or a version of the judge that no longer exists. ## Strengths - The judge prompt is published in full (Appendix C.3, and as `prompts.py` in the repository), including the per-category scoring rubrics. Anyone can inspect exactly what the judge was told to reward, which is more transparency than most model-as-a-judge work offers. - The raw judge outputs and the evaluation set are publicly downloadable, so third parties can re-aggregate the scores under different rules rather than taking Table 1 on faith. - Results are reported per category (Table 1, Figure 3), not only as a single aggregate win rate, so a system that is strong overall but weak on, say, complex pronunciation is visible as such. - The authors run sensitivity analyses that many benchmark papers skip: swapping the judge across five models (Kendall's W = 0.97, §4.3) and swapping the voice within a system (§4.4). Whatever one thinks of the conclusions drawn from them, the experiments themselves are the right ones to run. - The problem the benchmark addresses is real: word error rate does not capture prosodic or expressive failure, and a hard, adversarial test set for TTS is something the field genuinely needs. ## Major concerns 1. The test items and the judge come from the same model, and this overlap is never discussed, let alone isolated. Of the 1,645 items, only 100 are human-written seeds (five categories drawn from the 140 published BASE-TTS samples). The remaining 91.5% were produced by LLM expansion and rewriting, and all of the depth rewrites — the transformations that generate three of every four items in the set — were performed by Gemini 2.5 Pro (Appendix A, Appendix C.1). The primary judge is also Gemini 2.5 Pro (§3.2). The judge is therefore grading systems on items written in its own generation style, against rubrics applied to its own rewrites. Model families are known to favour outputs resembling their own; whether or not that effect is large here, a benchmark whose item generator and judge are the same model must at minimum acknowledge the confound and ideally report a control (for example, judge performance on the human-seed subset alone, or a cross-family generator/judge pairing). Neither appears anywhere in the paper. 2. The claim of high correlation with human preference rests on eight data points, eight annotators, and annotators who do not agree well with each other. The headline figure, Spearman ρ = 90.5% (Table 3b), is a correlation between rankings of eight models, not between per-item judgements; with n = 8, the statistic is extremely coarse. The human study behind it used 8 annotators and 512 audio pairs (§4.6), and the annotators' agreement with one another is Krippendorff's α = 0.5073, which the authors themselves describe as weak-to-moderate (Appendix D). A gold standard that is itself this unstable cannot certify a judge to the precision the headline number implies. Two further details sharpen the concern: all four judges evaluated in Table 3b return exactly the same ρ (90.5%), which suggests the metric cannot discriminate between judges at this sample size; and the annotators' backgrounds (employees, crowdworkers, native speakers, listeners with speech expertise) are never stated. Please report per-item agreement between judge and humans, the number of models and pairs behind the correlation, and who the annotators were. 3. Part of the measured human–machine agreement is built in by construction. The judging instructions given to the human annotators were adapted from the model judge's own prompt (§4.6.1). Annotators were therefore taught to evaluate using the machine's rubric before their agreement with the machine was measured. Agreement obtained this way shows that humans can be trained to apply the judge's criteria; it does not independently validate that the judge's criteria match unaided human preference. title: SUPRA: Synthesizing Amyloid PET from MRI and Plasma Biomarkers with an Explicit Regional SUVR Prior
abstract: Amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) quantifies brain amyloid-$β$ as a standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR), but is costly and not widely available. Structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is routine, and plasma biomarkers such as phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) are becoming practical. Synthesizing amyloid PET from MRI alone is ill-posed, because brain anatomy reveals little about amyloid burden. We present SUPRA (SUVR prior-guided amyloid synthesis), which divides this task between MRI and plasma biomarkers. A regression maps the plasma panel to regional SUVR levels, painted onto the subject's MRI segmentation as an explicit prior. A 3D network then adds a residual correction guided by MRI. The output is in absolute SUVR, and the model also runs on p-tau217 alone. On the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort (111 test pairs), SUPRA reaches a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 23.4 dB, against at most 20.7 dB for four published models, and rank correlations of 0.56 to 0.67 with true SUVR in the composite cortex, an early-accumulation region and the striatum, against at most 0.24. In a second, cognitively unimpaired cohort with other plasma platforms (143 test pairs), it reaches 22.8 dB and 0.32 to 0.61, against at most 21.4 dB and 0.20. Its area under the curve for amyloid positivity is 0.91 and 0.82, against at most 0.63. Ablations show that plasma supplies the amyloid information and the network the image quality. Combining MRI with a blood test yields synthetic amyloid PET that is realistic and tracks burden across regions.

title: Relation Before Action: Explicit Relation Modeling for Latent Action Pretraining
abstract: Learning latent actions from unlabeled video sequences offers a promising way to acquire reusable action representations without relying on embodiment-specific control annotations. However, existing latent-action pretraining approaches commonly couple the modeling of visual transitions with action inference, directly mapping paired observations or derived transition cues into latent action codes. This formulation leaves two distinct tasks entangled: characterizing the relational structure of an observed transition and abstracting it into a compact action representation. We propose RELACT, a relation-first framework that explicitly separates transition relation modeling from predictive action abstraction. RELACT first constructs a structured relation representation R that captures how visual elements and their interactions evolve across observations. It then infers a compact, state-conditioned stochastic latent action U, whose predictive effects are learned through action-conditioned latent dynamics. The resulting action representation can be grounded in native control spaces for model-based planning or used to supervise downstream embodied policies. Extensive experiments across in-domain and out-of-domain image-goal navigation, goal-conditioned manipulation, and downstream policy adaptation demonstrate improved predictive action representations and consistent gains in planning and control, supporting the effectiveness and generality of relation-first latent action pretraining.

title: ClusterVAD: Threshold-Free Unsupervised Voice Activity Detection with Pre-Trained Neural Representations
abstract: Voice activity detection (VAD) is one of the first steps in speech processing pipelines, from transcription and diarization to speech language models. Supervised detectors need labelled data and inherit the domain and annotation conventions of their training corpora. Existing unsupervised detectors rely on hand-crafted acoustic features which cannot benefit from data and degrade in far-field, noisy or atypical speech. We propose ClusterVAD, an unsupervised VAD built on frozen speech foundation model representations. Fitted once on a small set of untranscribed speech, it clusters the representations and labels each cluster as speech or non-speech with sonority, an acoustic measure. At inference, a frame-level speech probability is computed from the cluster assignments, and a two-state hidden Markov model fitted to each recording enables threshold-free detection. Across benchmarks covering meetings, far-field and noisy recordings, Mandarin and dysarthric speech, ClusterVAD obtains the lowest detection error on pause-level references and is competitive on speaker turn-level references. These results indicate that speech foundation models inherently capture the distinction between speech and non-speech, which can be leveraged without training a detector.

title: OmniEVIE: Evidence-Vector-Informed Embedding for Multi-modal Retrieval
abstract: Multimodal retrieval must match dense pages, fine-grained entities, ordered video, and agent tools and memory. Single-vector embeddings lose local evidence, cross-encoders reread every recalled item online, and uncompressed late interaction is too large to serve. We present OmniEVIE, a 4.5B multi-vector embedding model covering text, images, visual documents, video, and tools with one compressed index and a three-stage retriever. Each record stores at most 128 int8 vectors of dimension 64 (9,472 bytes, or 8.82 GiB per million records), providing a mean vector, 1-bit signs, and int8 multi-vectors for coarse, middle, and final search while localizing each hit to a page region or video interval. Training, merging, indexing, and retrieval are co-designed: all tasks share one retrieval format, a three-grade evidence check removes false negatives, dynamic sampling follows the baseline-teacher gap, candidates are compressed with ST-HAC during training to match the index, stage-wise and specialist models are merged by parameter block, and a saliency gate with a noise floor refines query scoring. Trained on public datasets, OmniEVIE scores 60.68 (full d=2048 sequence) and 60.06 (K128 x d64 int8 index) on MMEB-V3 (190 tasks), 77.96 on MMEB-V2 (78 tasks), and 62.96 on ViDoRe V3 (48 tasks). On 1M and 5M records, a single-thread query takes 54.2 ms and 120.2 ms (11.1x and 25.3x faster than exact 4096-d single-vector search; 236x and 532x faster than full int8 MaxSim). Video is encoded directly from frames without a parsing model: on QVHighlights (1,083 queries), the peak falls inside the labeled segment for 78.0% of queries and the returned span (18% of video length) intersects it for 94.3% vs. 44.9% random. Weights and code: https://huggingface.co/tencent/OmniEVIE-4B and https://github.com/Tencent/OmniEVIE.

title: Local Indices Are Not Enough: Synchrony and Global Information in Bandit Algorithms
abstract: Standard index-based stochastic bandit algorithms such as KL-UCB and Thompson Sampling achieve optimal $O(\log T)$ regret over a horizon $T$. The former uses the global timestep to construct each arm's index, while the latter samples each arm's belief distribution at every timestep. The necessity of global information and synchronous index updates for achieving optimal regret has not been examined yet. In this paper, we investigate the fundamental limits of asynchronous local index algorithms---those that recalculate an arm's index only upon pulling it, using solely that arm's own reward history and a local randomness budget. We prove that no such algorithm can achieve $O(\log T)$ regret across all bandit instances. We then analyse the functional equations arising from asynchronous updates, and show that the achievable regret lies in a sub-polynomial, super-polylogarithmic regime. We propose an asynchronous local index policy whose regret upper bound also lies in this regime. Turning to synchronous local algorithms, which sample every arm's index at all timesteps as in Thompson Sampling, we show that a locally determined randomness budget per arm suffices to retain $O(\log T)$ regret, demonstrating that synchrony, albeit with some randomness, is essential to the optimality of Thompson Sampling.

title: Steerable by Design: Conditional Pretraining for Robust Control of Language Models
abstract: Our goal is to build language models that are steerable by design. Today's language models are pretrained with next-token prediction, which relegates alignment and control to the final 1% of training tokens or inference-time interventions. These models repurpose a single input channel for both instructions and data, leading to common failure modes where the model mistakenly treats data as instructions such as intentional jailbreaks and unintentional in-context alignment drift. To correct this, we propose a pretraining method and architecture that separates the two from the very start, producing Mancelle-3B. An encoder processes high-level semantic features of upcoming text with cross-attention that prevents the token stream from writing back into this control channel. During pretraining, the model learns to rely on these features to predict the next token, turning the channel into an effective handle for steering the model. Mancelle-3B steers more strongly than prompt- and activation-based methods on comparable open models while maintaining fluency, and it withstands adversarial black-box and soft-prompt counter-steering that defeats those baselines. We reproduce this against a more controlled baseline with Mancelle-400M. Our results show that robust control can be built into language models if we do so early and intentionally.

title: Worth the Wait? How Response Time and Streaming Shape Judgments of Generative AI Answers and Chatbot Engagement
abstract: Answers from generative AI chatbots built on large language models (LLMs) now arrive at very different speeds: reasoning models deliberate before replying, while response caches can return a stored answer at once. Blind preference votes, which rank these models, are read as judgments of their text, and if delivery matters, faster answers are expected to gain. Research on the labor illusion and on how text appears on screen suggests instead that an answer which unfolds as it is written is credited over the same answer shown at once. We test these accounts with three sources of variation in natural use. First, compar:IA, a French government chatbot arena, answered repeated prompts, by a random draw, either with a fresh answer streamed as it was written or with a stored earlier answer from the same model, shown at once. Within the same prompt, a replay lowered an answer's chance of winning a decisive blind vote by 25.8 percentage points. The same stored text won 57% of its decisive votes when streamed and 29% when replayed, and voters called it less complete, more superficial and more often incorrect when replayed. Second, provider congestion slowed streamed answers. In 324,029 conversations, slower answers earned no detectable net credit in the vote, but a slower first exchange made visitors less likely to ask a follow-up question. Third, in 4,378,514 WildChat replies from everyday ChatGPT use, replies slowed by congestion made users less likely to continue. Delivery moved blind votes, in the direction opposite to the one the arena's designers expected, while waiting cost follow-up questions that a comparison between two answers cannot register when both are slow.
